frameworks.name: Document-Demonstrate-Duplicate
frameworks.definition: A three-step training method: (1) document the exact checklist of steps while performing the task; (2) demonstrate it step-by-step to the employee; (3) have the employee duplicate it in front of you, iterating the checklist until replication is perfect.

frameworks.name: Stop-Start-Keep Feedback Frame
frameworks.definition: A behavior-change feedback structure: tell a person what behavior to stop doing, what new behavior to start doing, and what current behavior to keep doing — in that order — to give actionable specificity rather than vague trait labels.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a business error results in a customer being net negative (e.g., traveling from Israel for an event that did not exist), a refund alone leaves the customer still net negative and does not restore goodwill; the company must over-compensate to actually make it right.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: customer experienced a concrete, tangible loss beyond the monetary value of the purchase (e.g., travel costs, time)
claims.mechanism: A refund returns money but not the sunk cost of the customer's actions; over-compensation restores the net-positive balance that goodwill requires.
bounded_by: Does not apply to low-stakes purchases where the only cost is the purchase price itself

claims.text: Alex Hormozi cites a Disney statistic that it takes 37 magical moments to overcome one tragic moment; he interprets the practical implication as: minimize tragic moments rather than engineering 37 compensating magic moments, because the recovery cost is asymmetric.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Positive experiences and negative experiences do not cancel linearly; one strongly negative event requires disproportionately many positive events to neutralize.

numbers.axis: number of positive moments required to offset one negative moment

anchors.value: requires 37 magical moments to overcome (Disney statistic)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that customers who have been wronged and then super-compensated beyond the wrong become the business's biggest ambassadors — stronger advocates than customers who never had a problem — because the over-compensation demonstrates company values in a way normal service never triggers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: the company must over-compensate materially, not merely issue an apology or refund
claims.mechanism: Extreme recovery signals organizational character and commitment in a high-stakes context that ordinary service cannot replicate, converting emotional negativity into emotional loyalty.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that high churn in group-based programs is primarily caused by low activation (low actual consumption of sessions), not by product quality; and that low consumption precedes and predicts high churn.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: group or semi-private coaching/training programs with recurring attendance model
claims.mechanism: Members who do not attend do not experience value; without experienced value, renewal motivation is absent and churn follows.

numbers.axis: member attendance rate in a semi-private coaching program

anchors.value: 7% of student body actually attending sessions
not specified — any material increase materially reduces churn

bounded_by: Does not apply to self-paced asynchronous products where consumption is not session-based

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends a structured individual onboarding sequence of four to six one-on-one sessions before transitioning new members into group sessions, framing the group as a prize to be earned rather than the default starting point, to drive higher initial engagement and long-term retention.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: semi-private or group coaching/training programs
members currently exhibiting low attendance and high churn
claims.mechanism: Individual onboarding creates personal buy-in and reduces disorientation; positioning group sessions as the graduated reward elevates their perceived value, increasing attendance motivation.

numbers.axis: number of individual onboarding sessions before group transition

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that the majority of entrepreneurs experiencing a business problem do not collect any data that precedes the problem, which forces them to cycle through hypothetical solutions indefinitely; collecting data first makes the solution path obvious.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Without preceding data, the root cause of the problem is unknown and any solution is a guess; data makes the causal chain visible and the correct intervention self-evident.

numbers.axis: frequency with which entrepreneurs have data preceding their problem

anchors.region: Hormozi's observed rate across intake conversations
anchors.value: 9 out of 10 do not collect relevant preceding data
tracking in place before the problem manifests

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the lowest risk-adjusted move in any business is to maximize what is already working — answering 'why can't we do more?' — before pivoting to a new customer type, channel, or business model; the only legitimate trigger for pursuing a new avatar is exhausting the existing one.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business already has a profitable, scaling acquisition channel and proven product
claims.mechanism: A new avatar requires a new offering and new acquisition — functionally a new business — so all existing problems recur with additional uncertainty layered on top, making the risk-adjusted return lower than solving the known constraint.
bounded_by: When the existing market is genuinely exhausted (all reachable customers acquired), expansion to new avatars becomes appropriate

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a business has a sales efficiency problem, that problem exists on every growth path (B2C and B2B) and must be solved on the current path rather than abandoned for a new one; switching to B2B to escape B2C sales efficiency problems moves the same problem to a harder environment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: consumer (B2C) business with proven paid acquisition channel (e.g., Facebook ads) and existing sales efficiency issues
claims.mechanism: Problems in the current model are inherited by any new model targeting a new customer type; B2B enterprise sales introduces additional complexity (more stakeholders, longer cycles) on top of the existing problem.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in B2B enterprise-level sales, increasing the number of stakeholders involved on both the buyer's side and the seller's side increases both conversion rate and customer retention, because each additional tie strengthens commitment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B enterprise sales with multiple decision-makers on buyer side
deal size sufficient to justify multi-stakeholder sales process
claims.mechanism: More stakeholders on both sides create more interpersonal ties; each tie is an additional commitment anchor that raises the cost of defection for both parties.

numbers.axis: number of touch points in B2B enterprise sales relative to B2C

bounded_by: Does not apply to self-serve or low-touch B2B software

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when a Facebook ads-driven B2C business reaches ad spend saturation (declining ROAS), the five levers to unlock further scale are: (1) better lead magnet, (2) better creative, (3) improved conversion rate optimization on landing pages, (4) improved sales efficiency, and (5) all four simultaneously; the difference between a business spending $5,000/day and $100,000/day profitably is execution quality across these four levers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Facebook ads as primary paid acquisition channel
business experiencing ROAS decline as spend increases
claims.mechanism: Ad platforms deliver diminishing returns on spend without proportional improvement in conversion infrastructure; upgrading funnel quality restores ROAS headroom.

numbers.axis: daily Facebook ad spend achievable profitably

anchors.region: high-quality execution across all four levers

claims.text: Alex Hormozi advises that identifying the single highest-leverage acquisition channel (measured by revenue-per-unit-time or revenue-per-dollar) and multiplying volume on that channel before adding new channels is the correct scaling sequence for a sub-$10M business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business doing meaningful revenue from one channel (e.g., speaking events) at very low volume (e.g., 1 per year)
claims.mechanism: When one channel has demonstrated high revenue per instance and low frequency, the same investment of time/money into more instances of that channel yields near-linear returns before saturation — a simpler and lower-risk path than opening new channels.

numbers.axis: speaking events per year as acquisition channel for professional service businesses

anchors.value: 270+ events per year, took Real from $200M to $1.2B revenue in 24 months

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a private equity portfolio owner with 14 heterogeneous companies faces a structural problem: too many companies to apply a hands-on value-add model, but not enough synergy across companies to benefit from a roll-up model; the path to $50M enterprise value requires choosing either concentrated focus (fewer companies, active management) or vertical integration (many companies of the same type with centralized costs and best-practice distribution).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: private equity portfolio with 14+ heterogeneous businesses
target exit of $50M enterprise value

numbers.axis: PE portfolio concentration models and typical fund sizes

anchors.value: 6-8 companies per fund with hands-on improvement team
only buys vertically integrated SaaS under $3M, runs 100+ deals/year with repeatable playbook
14 heterogeneous companies — too many for value-add, too diverse for roll-up

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in a roll-up private equity strategy, buying 10 similar businesses enables centralizing costs (reducing the bottom line across all) and distributing best practices from each individual business to all others, producing an enterprise value multiple far exceeding the sum of individual valuations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: portfolio companies in the same industry or vertical
claims.mechanism: Cost centralization reduces per-unit overhead for all portfolio companies simultaneously; cross-company best-practice transfer raises performance of weaker companies toward the best-performing ones, compounding EBITDA gains across the portfolio.

numbers.axis: enterprise value relationship: individual purchase price vs. combined exit price

anchors.region: individual purchase prices for 10 similar businesses
combined exit value after roll-up synergies

bounded_by: Requires the businesses to be in the same vertical to achieve cost and knowledge synergies; does not apply to heterogeneous portfolios

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a supply-constrained service business (high demand, insufficient trained staff) should be reframed as a recruiting business: the primary operational activity is recruiting and retaining the scarce supply of producers, not delivering the service itself.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business with more demand than it can fulfill
constrained by scarcity of licensed or trained practitioners (e.g., physical therapists, cleaners)
claims.mechanism: When demand is not the binding constraint, adding marketing spend does not grow revenue; only expanding the supply of producers does, making recruiting the highest-ROI activity.
bounded_by: Does not apply to demand-constrained businesses (sufficient staff, insufficient customers)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that supply-constrained businesses dramatically underinvest in recruiting incentives relative to the gross profit each additional producer generates; businesses that would invest $100,000 in financial markets for $10,000 return refuse to pay $10,000 commission on a hire generating $300,000+ gross profit annually.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: supply-constrained service businesses where each additional practitioner generates meaningful gross profit per year
claims.mechanism: The ROI on recruiting investment (gross profit per hire divided by recruiting cost) is typically several orders of magnitude higher than financial market returns; the psychological barrier is that recruiting feels like a cost rather than a capital deployment.

numbers.axis: gross profit per additional physical therapist hire per year vs. recruiting incentive willingness to pay

anchors.region: gross profit per physical therapist per year (example business)
typical referral bonus that 'feels' like enough
Hormozi's recommended referral incentive to actually move people
analogous financial market: $100K invested at 10% return

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that trait labels like 'lazy' or 'patient' are not useful in managing or training employees because they are unobservable; effective behavior change requires decomposing the trait into specific observable behaviors and giving explicit stop/start directives.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: managing or training employees
giving corrective feedback
claims.mechanism: Trait labels ('be more patient') give no actionable information because they point to an identity state, not a behavior; the employee cannot change an abstract trait, only a specific action. Observable behavior directives ('respond to Slack within 1 hour') provide a concrete target that can be measured and reinforced.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the Document-Demonstrate-Duplicate training framework scales skill transfer to employees; the common failure mode is that most companies do not train — they hire for inherent skill, observe performance, and fire those who lack it — which treats training as luck rather than process.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: companies hiring for roles with learnable skills
bounded_by: Complex trait development (e.g., transforming an unkind person into a kind one) has high sub-skill cost; trait gaps measured in months to train vs. skill gaps measured in days

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in hiring, the goal is to minimize the skill deficiency of the candidate relative to the role requirements, rather than finding a perfect candidate; 'traits' are simply clusters of skills with different training timelines, and a candidate with two days of training needed on sales but two months on kindness should be evaluated against hiring a kind candidate who needs two days of sales training.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: role has a clearly defined skill set
company has training capacity
claims.mechanism: Skills have different training timelines; hiring the candidate with the smallest total training burden minimizes time-to-full-productivity.

examples.text: At an Acquisition.com event, a memo about a schedule change was not communicated to one salesperson, who sold six people into an event that no longer existed. Customers arrived, including one who flew from Israel. Rather than refunding them, the team spent the day with all six and took them out to dinner. The Israeli attendee later returned and gave a heartfelt testimonial, becoming an ambassador for the company. Hormozi uses this as proof that over-compensation converts wronged customers into the strongest advocates.

A semi-private coaching program participant reported 50% churn across both their $195/month and $595/four-month offer tiers (weighted 30% churn), tracing back to only 7% of the student body actually attending sessions. Hormozi diagnosed low activation as the root cause and recommended individual onboarding before group entry as the fix.

A career coaching business doing $7.2M in revenue with $2M profit wanted to add B2B enterprise sales because they had hit $1M in a month and felt it was time to diversify. They were spending $3,000-$5,000 per day on Facebook ads. Hormozi identified that their actual constraint was sales efficiency, not avatar exhaustion, and that their scale potential on B2C alone extended to $50,000-$100,000/day in ad spend — a 10-30x increase before any new channel was warranted.

A professional book publishing services company doing $1M revenue had tried all acquisition channels — referrals, organic, speaking, cold email, Facebook ads — and identified speaking engagements as generating significant revenue per event, yet was only doing one per year. Hormozi immediately advised targeting 50 speaking events the following year, citing Tamir Poleg of Real (a publicly traded real estate brokerage) who did 66 speeches in Q4 alone and grew the company from $200M to $1.2B in revenue within 24 months by speaking at real estate events as the primary agent-acquisition channel.

A health and wellness business (physical therapy plus personal training, serving 35-45 year old athletes, $3M+ revenue) faced a shortage of practitioners with 16,000 open positions industry-wide and more patient demand than it could serve. The founder was considering raising prices toward a concierge model or starting an e-commerce business on the side. Hormozi reframed the problem: the business was actually a physical therapist recruiting business that happened to deliver therapy. The constraint was recruiting, not pricing strategy or business model.

An ex-gym-owner turned real estate investor started a cleaning company to clean his Airbnbs, then began selling cleaning services externally. His customer acquisition cost was $25, making demand trivially easy to acquire. His constraint was finding English-speaking cleaners who were reliable, honest, and willing to work for $15/hour. Hormozi used this story to illustrate supply-constrained vs. demand-constrained businesses: fitness is typically demand-constrained (hard to get people to commit to gym attendance), while home cleaning is supply-constrained (easy to get customers, hard to find workers).

During the leader training discussion, Hormozi gave the example of a manager repeatedly telling an employee named Sarah that she was 'lazy' without change. He walked through the diagnostic: the manager observed specific behaviors (Sarah not responding to Slack messages, going offline before 9pm) and ascribed the label 'lazy' to those behaviors. The fix was to replace the label with specific directives: 'respond to Slack messages within X, enable notifications on both devices.' Asking whether anything would block this revealed Sarah was covering for a laid-off colleague whose role hadn't been backfilled.

practices.text: Book a meeting from a meeting (BAMFAM): at the end of every session, pull up calendars with all attendees and book the next session before anyone leaves.
Send automated reminders for every scheduled session, plus a manual personal outreach from the session facilitator to the expected attendees before each call.

When managing a heterogeneous PE portfolio, run an 80/20 analysis: identify the 20% of companies driving 80% of enterprise value, go fully passive or return equity on the rest, and double down on the high-value subset.
When a recruiting referral incentive is not generating referrals, keep raising the dollar amount until referrals occur; the market will signal what the incentive threshold needs to be.

Apply the Core Four acquisition methods to recruiting producers (physical therapists, cleaners, etc.) the same way you apply them to acquiring customers: warm outreach, cold outreach, paid ads, organic content, plus headhunter channels and existing staff referrals.
When giving corrective feedback to employees, use the Stop-Start-Keep frame: 'I need you to stop doing X, start doing Y, and keep doing Z' — give explicit behavior directives, not trait labels.
